blurb: Prefill and decode, batching, quantization, speculative decoding and sampling strategies.

cards.title: Two very different phases

steps.p: The whole prompt is processed in one parallel pass, filling the KV cache. It is compute-bound and sets time-to-first-token.
Each output token then needs its own forward pass, reading all the weights. It is memory-bound and sets tokens per second.
Some even run prefill and decode on separate GPUs, because the two phases want different hardware trade-offs.

cards.aside: When a reply starts slowly, think prefill. When it streams slowly, think decode.

cards.q: For a long prompt, time-to-first-token is dominated by…
cards.why: Prefill. The model must process every prompt token before it can predict the first output token. Long documents mean long prefill.

cards.statement: APIs typically charge more per output token than per input token.
cards.why: True, often 3–5× more. Input tokens are processed in parallel; output tokens are generated one at a time, tying up the GPU much longer per token.

options: Waiting until a full batch arrives
Adding and removing requests from the running batch at every step
Running one request at a time
cards.why: Swapping requests in and out. Without it, a batch waits for its longest reply to finish. With it, finished requests leave and new ones join immediately.

cards.title: vLLM borrowed an idea from operating systems — virtual memory paging — to manage the KV cache.
cards.detail: Its PagedAttention (2023) stores the cache in small fixed-size blocks instead of one big contiguous chunk per request. The authors reported earlier systems wasted 60–80% of KV cache memory to fragmentation.

cards.statement: Prompt caching lets a provider skip recomputing a prompt prefix it has seen recently.
cards.why: True. If many requests share a long system prompt or document, its KV cache can be reused. Providers pass on the savings as discounted cached-input pricing.

cards.title: Shrinking the numbers

steps.p: Weights trained in 16-bit can be stored in 8 or 4 bits, with a scale factor for each small group of weights.
Decode speed is limited by reading weights, so a 4-bit model generates tokens far faster than a 16-bit one on the same hardware.
Methods like GPTQ and AWQ choose roundings that minimize error on real data, so 4-bit models lose surprisingly little.

cards.aside: Quantization is why a capable model can run on a laptop.

cards.q: A 70B model quantized to 4 bits needs roughly how much memory for its weights?
cards.why: About 35 GB. 70 billion × 0.5 bytes. At 16-bit it would be 140 GB. Real files run slightly larger because of scale factors.

cards.statement: Quantizing a large model to 4 bits typically destroys its quality.
cards.why: False. Good 4-bit methods usually cost only a small drop on benchmarks. Quality falls off more sharply around 3 bits and below.

cards.q: Why did naive 8-bit quantization of large models initially fail?
options: 8 bits is too small for any number
A few activation features had huge outlier values that rounding destroyed
cards.why: Outliers. Dettmers et al. (LLM.int8, 2022) found that above roughly 6B parameters, a few feature dimensions carry very large values. Handling them separately in higher precision fixed it.

cards.title: Ollama runs models using llama.cpp, a project that started as a weekend hack to run LLaMA on a MacBook.
cards.detail: Georgi Gerganov released llama.cpp in March 2023. Its GGUF quantized format became a standard way to run models locally on CPUs and Apple silicon.

cards.q: Weight-only quantization speeds up single-user generation mainly by…
options: Reducing the bytes read from memory per token
cards.why: Fewer bytes moved. Decode is memory-bound, so halving bytes per weight roughly doubles tokens per second — even though weights are expanded back to 16-bit for the math.

cards.title: Guess cheaply, verify in bulk

steps.p: A fast draft model guesses the next few tokens — say five.

steps.h: The big model checks them all at once
steps.p: The large model scores all five positions in one forward pass, which costs about the same as generating one token.
Draft tokens are accepted until the first one the big model disagrees with; it supplies the correction and the cycle repeats.

cards.aside: With the right acceptance rule, output follows exactly the big model's distribution — the speedup is free.

cards.q: Why is checking five draft tokens about as cheap as generating one?
options: Decode is memory-bound, so the weights read once can score several positions in parallel
cards.why: Spare compute. Single-token decode leaves most arithmetic units idle while waiting on memory. Scoring extra positions uses that idle compute with the same weight read.

cards.statement: Speculative decoding changes what the large model would have output.
cards.why: False. With rejection sampling, accepted tokens follow exactly the big model's distribution. It is a pure speed trick.

cards.q: What mainly determines how much speculative decoding helps?
options: How often the big model accepts the draft's guesses
cards.why: Acceptance rate. Predictable text — code boilerplate, common phrasing — gets accepted often and speeds up a lot. Surprising text gets rejected and gains little.

cards.title: Some models are trained to predict several future tokens at once.
cards.detail: Approaches like Medusa add extra prediction heads, and DeepSeek-V3 used a multi-token prediction objective. The extra predictions can serve as built-in drafts for speculative decoding.

cards.statement: Greedy decoding — always picking the single most likely token — always produces the most likely full response.
cards.why: False. The best next token can lead to a worse overall sequence. Greedy is locally optimal; beam search explores more but tends to produce bland chat text.

cards.title: Sampling knobs

steps.p: Divides the scores before softmax. Below 1 sharpens toward the top choice; above 1 flattens toward randomness.
Sample only from the k most likely tokens, cutting off the long tail of unlikely ones.
Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. The set grows when the model is unsure and shrinks when it is confident.

cards.aside: Top-p adapts to the situation, which is why it is more common than a fixed top-k.

cards.q: With top-p = 0.9, the model samples from…
options: The smallest set of tokens whose combined probability reaches 90%
cards.why: The nucleus. If one token has 95% probability, only it is eligible. If the distribution is flat, dozens might be.

cards.q: Beam search is common in translation but rare in chatbots because it…
options: Tends to produce bland, repetitive text in open-ended generation
cards.why: Degeneration. Maximizing likelihood favors safe, generic and repetitive phrasing. Human writing is less probable than what beam search picks.

cards.statement: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees identical output on every run of an API.
cards.why: False. Batching with other requests and floating-point ordering on GPUs can change results slightly. Exact determinism needs special engineering.

cards.title: Structured output modes can guarantee a model returns valid JSON.
cards.detail: Constrained decoding masks out every token that would break the required schema at each step, so the model literally cannot produce invalid output.

cards.title: Match temperature to the task
cards.body: Extracting facts, writing code or classifying wants low temperature for consistency. Brainstorming and creative writing benefit from higher temperature for variety.
cards.challenge: Ask the same brainstorming question at a low and a high temperature (or "be conventional" vs "be surprising") and compare.
